prompt: Lia and Davi both average 35 minutes per delivery. What does that tell you about how dependable each one is?
hint: Look at how far the times sit from 35.

choices.text: That they are equally dependable
choices.why: Lia's times stay within 33 to 36 minutes and Davi's range from 22 to 44: equal means, very unequal dependability.

choices.text: Nothing: dependability is about spread, which the mean ignores
choices.why: Right. The mean describes the centre; how far the values stray from it is a separate question.

choices.text: That Davi is more dependable, as his times include the fastest
choices.why: Fast and slow deliveries mixed together are the opposite of dependable.

choices.text: That both will meet a 40-minute promise every time
choices.why: Davi took 44 minutes twice in eight deliveries.

prompt: Horta's twelve delivery times run from 27.5 to 61.0 minutes. What is the range, in minutes?
Lia has one delivery of 58 minutes after a flat tyre; her other seven stay between 33 and 36. What happens to her range?
hint: The range is the largest minus the smallest.

choices.text: It barely changes, since seven of eight values are the same
choices.why: The range uses only the two extremes, and one of them just moved by 22 minutes.

choices.text: It doubles
choices.why: From 3 to 25 is more than eight times, not double.

choices.text: It jumps from 3 to 25 minutes
choices.why: Right. One unusual value controls the range completely: 58 − 33 = 25.

choices.text: It falls, because the mean rises
choices.why: The range does not depend on the mean at all.

prompt: Why are Lia's range over 8 deliveries and her range over 800 not comparable?
hint: What happens to the chance of catching a very slow delivery as you look at more?

choices.text: More data gives more chances of an extreme value
choices.why: Right. The range keeps growing with the amount of data even if the courier never changes.

choices.text: The range of 800 values has to be divided by 100 first
choices.why: There is no such correction; the range is simply larger with more data, and no division fixes that reliably.

choices.text: Ranges are only defined for samples under 30
choices.why: A range exists for any amount of data; the problem is that it grows with it.

choices.text: Her deliveries surely got slower over time
choices.why: Nothing says so; the range would grow even if her deliveries stayed exactly as they are.

prompt: Why does the variance square the deviations instead of simply averaging them?

choices.text: Squaring makes the numbers smaller and easier to read
choices.why: Squaring makes most deviations larger, and the units become squared, which is harder to read.

choices.text: Plain deviations from the mean add up to zero
choices.why: Right. Squaring makes every deviation positive, so the fast and slow deliveries stop cancelling.

choices.text: So that values below the mean count more than values above it
choices.why: Squaring treats −9 and +9 identically; both become 81.

choices.text: To convert minutes into seconds
choices.why: Squaring minutes gives square minutes, not seconds.

prompt: Four deliveries took 30, 34, 36 and 40 minutes; their mean is 35. What is their sample variance?
hint: Squared deviations 25, 1, 1 and 25; divide their sum by 3.

prompt: Davi's variance is 66. In what units is it?
hint: What happens to the unit when you square a number of minutes?

choices.text: Minutes, like the data
choices.why: The deviations were squared, and so were their units.

choices.text: It has no units, being a ratio
choices.why: The coefficient of variation has no units; the variance is not a ratio.

choices.text: Percentage points
choices.why: Nothing in the calculation produces a percentage.

choices.text: Minutes squared
choices.why: Right. That is why the standard deviation, its square root, is the one reported.

prompt: A sample variance is 49 square minutes. What is the standard deviation, in minutes?
Using the four deliveries of 30, 34, 36 and 40 minutes, what is the sample standard deviation? Give two decimal places.
A report gives the standard deviation of basket values as −12.4. What should you conclude?
hint: What is a square root of an average of squares?

choices.text: Baskets mostly fell below the mean
choices.why: Position relative to the mean has no sign in a standard deviation: every deviation is squared.

choices.text: There is a mistake
choices.why: Right. A standard deviation is the square root of an average of squares, so it cannot be negative.

choices.text: The spread is very small
choices.why: Very small spread is a standard deviation close to zero, not below it.

choices.text: The data was divided by n rather than n − 1
choices.why: Either divisor gives a positive number; the choice changes the size, never the sign.

prompt: Match each spreadsheet function to what it returns for a column of values.
hint: S for sample, P for population.

pairs.right: the standard deviation, dividing by n − 1
the standard deviation, dividing by n

prompt: Why does dividing a sample's sum of squares by n tend to underestimate the population variance?
hint: From which point are the deviations measured?

choices.text: Samples always contain fewer extreme values than populations
choices.why: A sample can contain extreme values; the bias comes from where the deviations are measured from.

choices.text: Deviations are measured from the sample's mean, which minimises them
choices.why: Right. The sample mean is the point that makes the sum of squares smallest, so it is a little too small on average.

choices.text: Because n is larger than the number of values
choices.why: n is the number of values.

choices.text: Because rounding errors accumulate over n values
choices.why: The bias appears with exact arithmetic too, as the population of three showed.

prompt: Five deviations from a sample mean are −4, 1, 2 and 3, and one more. What must the fifth be?
hint: Deviations from the mean add up to zero.

prompt: With n values and their mean fixed, only n − 1 deviations are free to vary. The number n − 1 is called the degrees of ___.
Horta wants the spread of its nine staff salaries, and only those nine people. Which divisor fits, and why?
hint: Is anybody being inferred about beyond the nine?

choices.text: n − 1, because every data set is a sample
choices.why: Not every data set is a sample. When the question is about exactly these nine, they are the population.

choices.text: n − 1, because nine is a small number
choices.why: The choice depends on whether you infer beyond the data, not on how many values there are.

choices.text: n: the nine are the whole population being described
choices.why: Right. There is nothing beyond the data to infer, so no correction for a sample mean is needed.

choices.text: Either, because the two give the same answer
choices.why: With nine values they differ noticeably: dividing by 8 instead of 9 raises the variance by an eighth.

prompt: A filling machine's bags have a mean of 500 g and a standard deviation of 4 g. What is the coefficient of variation, as a decimal?
Delivery times have a CV of 0.25 and baskets a CV of 0.75. What does that comparison say?
hint: What does dividing by the mean remove?

choices.text: Baskets have a standard deviation three times that of delivery times
choices.why: The standard deviations are in different units and cannot be compared directly; the CV compares them relative to each mean.

choices.text: Baskets vary three times as much, relative to their size
choices.why: Right. The CV removes the units: each spread is measured as a share of its own mean.

choices.text: Delivery times are measured three times more accurately
choices.why: The CV here describes how much the quantities vary, not how precisely they are measured.

choices.text: Baskets have three times as many outliers
choices.why: The CV does not count anything; it is a ratio of spread to mean.

prompt: Why is a coefficient of variation of temperatures in °C meaningless?
hint: Lesson 2: which scales allow a ratio?

choices.text: Temperatures have too little spread for a CV
choices.why: The amount of spread is not the issue; the zero of the scale is.

choices.text: The standard deviation of a temperature cannot be computed
choices.why: It can: differences in °C are meaningful, so the standard deviation is fine. The mean in the denominator is the trouble.

choices.text: Its mean depends on an arbitrary zero, so the ratio does too
choices.why: Right. In Fahrenheit the same days give a different mean and so a different CV. A CV needs a ratio scale.

choices.text: Temperature is ordinal
choices.why: Celsius is interval: its differences are equal steps.

prompt: Put the steps of computing a sample standard deviation in order.
hint: The table in the variance section, row by row.
items: Subtract the mean from each value
Add the squares and divide by n − 1
trap: Taking the square root before adding would give the mean absolute deviation's cousin, not the standard deviation.
